The first thing my father asked me to steal was a tree. He called on a Tuesday, while I was eating lunch over the sink.

“Bring the shovel with the red handle,” he said.

“Are we burying something?”

“Other way around.”

The tree was a pear, not much taller than he was, growing behind the house where I grew up. My father had sold the house in March. It was now November, and the new owners had put a trampoline exactly where our kitchen table used to be, if you counted through the wall.

“Did you ask them?” I said.

“I left a message.”

“When?”

He took a pair of work gloves out of his coat and examined them, as if the answer might be printed inside.

My mother had planted the pear tree the year she gave up smoking. She bought it with the money she’d saved in a mayonnaise jar and spent the rest on a pink blouse that made my father say, every time she wore it, “Well, look at you.” The blouse lasted longer than the resolution. The tree, which was supposed to produce two varieties of pear on the same trunk, had produced one small, very hard pear in twelve years. My mother put it on the windowsill and waited for it to ripen until my father used it to prop open the bathroom door.

The new owners weren’t home. There was a plastic dinosaur on the back step, flattened at the hips from having been shut in the door. My father picked it up and stood it on the railing.

“We can go to a nursery,” I said. “You can get a bigger one.”

“I don’t know where I’d put a bigger one.”

I had no idea where he meant to put this one. His new apartment was on the third floor, over a bakery. He insisted you couldn’t smell the bread from up there, although the first time I visited he opened the door and said, before he said hello, “They’ve burnt something.”

I put the shovel in the ground. The soil was wet enough to come up in slabs. Beneath the sod was a piece of blue china, and beneath that a worm. My father moved the worm out of the way with one finger.

“You know she didn’t even like pears,” he said.

“I know.”

“She liked those little ones in the tin.”

“Those are pears.”

“Well, she liked the tin.”

We dug a circle, then a bigger circle. Roots kept turning up where roots had no business being, under the path and out toward the clothesline. I had thought of a tree as a thing with a top and a bottom, and had brought a tarp sized for approximately that idea. My father sat on the overturned wheelbarrow and held one end of the tarp in his lap so it wouldn’t blow away.

At half past three, a woman came through the side gate with a child in a reflective vest. She had a bag of groceries in each hand. The child stopped short at the hole.

“Is it dead?” he asked.

“No,” said my father.

The woman set the bags down. A leek stuck out of one, trailing rainwater from its leaves.

“I got your message,” she said.

My father wiped his gloves on his trousers. “We can fill it in.”

“Oh, you can have it. I thought you meant the big tree.”

We all looked across the yard at the ash, which was taller than the house. I tried to imagine my father leaving a message about coming round to collect it. Evidently the woman had tried, too, and had got far enough to wonder what kind of equipment he might bring.

“Hang on,” she said. “He made something for it.”

The child went inside and came back with a square of plywood on a string. PEARS 5p, it said. On the back, in smaller letters, was NO CREDIT.

“He saw the label,” she said. The nursery tag was still looped around a branch, bleached nearly blank. “He’s been checking it before school.”

My father took the sign. “Five pence apiece?”

“For a bag,” the child said.

“You’ll want to have another think about that.”

The woman picked up her groceries. The child watched my father turn the sign over twice, then said, “You can keep it,” in the tone of someone who has given away a pet and hopes to hear where it will sleep.

I waited for my father to say thank you. Instead he got up and went to the hole. With the toe of his boot he nudged a slab of sod back into place. It sat too high. He stamped on it, then stamped again.

“Have you turned the heating on yet?” he asked the woman.

“We have. It makes a racket.”

“That’ll be the pipe behind the cupboard. There’s a wooden wedge on top of the boiler. I took it out for the inspection and forgot to put it back.” He showed her how wide the wedge was with his thumb and finger. Then he told her where the stopcock was, which window needed lifting before you pulled it shut, and why she shouldn’t pay anybody to come out about the extractor fan until she’d tried turning it off at the wall. I’d heard most of this before. The thing about the wedge was new to me.

The child helped us push the dirt back with the sides of his boots. Then he hung his sign on a low branch, where the price was legible from the kitchen.

On the way home my father carried the muddy shovel across his knees. We stopped outside the bakery. The lights were still on, and a woman inside was putting the unsold rolls into a paper sack.

“Do you want me to come up?” I asked.

“Yes,” he said, without looking over. Then he opened his door a little, closed it again, and said, “Actually, let’s go in here first. I’ve never been.”
